articles.headline: Cumulative Dean's List Rises By 33
articles.body:
150 Students Appear On Total Listings

The second semester cumulative Dean's List, containing 128 names, shows an increase of 33 over last semester's list, and an increase of 25 over the previous semester's list, according to figures released by George W. Burns, dean of the University.

The semester Dean's List, with 22 names, shows a decrease of 11 over last semester but an increase of 16 over the previous semester.

To receive the cumulative honor, seniors must have a point average of 3.4 or better. juniors a 3.35 or better and sophomores a 3.3 or better.

Honors Paper Dropped

The honors paper required of seniors in previous semesters is no longer necessary for placement on the Dean's List.

The semester Dean's List includes seniors with a semester point average of 3.6 or better, juniors with a 3.55 or better and sophomores with a 3.5 or better.

The names of 39 seniors, 37 juniors and 52 sophomores appear on this semester's cumulative list. Last year, nine seniors, 33 juniors and 53 sophomores appeared on the list.

Seniors Listed

Seniors on the cumulative list are as follows: Carol Anderson, Judy Blackburn, Sarah Blackmun, Alain Cavanie, Sarah Conner, Russ Dancy, Don Eastridge, Sue Flemming, Barb Follmer, Susan Fraser and Larry Fulmer.

Also, Dick Gigax, Willy Good, Carol Goodspeed, Pat Gray, Kanji Haitani, Dick Hattwick, Dick Hodge, Margaret Hoehn, Ray Hopkins, Elaine Hunsicker, Jack Kangas, Lucile Kossodo, Margery MacLeod, Bonnie McDonald, Melvyn Magree, Ken Morris and John Mumma.

articles.headline: Alpha Sigma Phi Wins Fraternity Song Fest
articles.body:
Alpha Sigma Phi fraternity won the annual Greek Week fraternity song fest Sunday night in Gray Chapel for the second year in a row.

Runner-up honors went to Delta Tau Delta fraternity, their sixth straight second place, while Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity took third, Merritt Rudolph, song fest coordinator, told the Transcript Monday.

Tom Clough, song director for the Alpha Sigs, received two trophies on behalf of his chapter. Steve Whitehead, Greek Week chairman, presented the permanent trophy from the song fest sponsor, Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia, national music fraternity.

Intermission entertainment was provided by Bob Nelson, as "Madstone the Magician," and by the Men's Triple Quartet, composed of members of the A Cappella Choir, which sang three numbers while the judges were making their decision.

Eleven of OWU's 13 fraternities competed, with Phi Delta Theta fraternity singing without entering the contest. Beta Sigma Tau and Sigma Phi Epsilon did not appear on the Gray Chapel stage.

The judges — John B. Ham, Wittenberg University; Richard Johnston, Capital University, and Dale K. Moore, Denison University — commented after the singing that some of the groups have "done credit to a college glee club," reported Rudolph.

articles.headline: OWU Enrollment Loss Varies Little
articles.body:
Little difference was recorded in the number of students who dropped out or entered the University this semester, as compared with figures for last year, according to information received from the offices of the deans of men and women.

At first semester's end, 25 upperclass men were dropped from the University because of low grades, as compared with 29 last year. No women students were dropped because of grades. However, Audrey M. Parker, dean of women, said that more women left during the first semester due to illness than ever before.

In addition to those dropped, 15 men and 26 women completed their studies at the end of the semester and graduated.

While a total of 66 students left the University in February, 26 new and returning men students and 12 new and returning women students began their studies here then, the deans' reports stated.

articles.headline: Hart, Esch Head Bijou, Transcript
articles.body:
New Transcript Staff To Take Over Apr. 6

Sophomores Ray Esch and Paul Hart were named editors of the Transcript and Le Bijou, respectively, by the joint student-faculty Publications Board last Friday afternoon.

Esch, an undeclared English major from Birmingham, Ala., moves up from his present position as news and associate editor of the student newspaper. The new editor, who was unopposed for the post, plans to have staff selections completed by next week, he said.

The Esch administration will assume command with the Apr. 16 issue of the Transcript.

Hart Unopposed

Hart, whose staff will begin planning on the new yearbook this spring, was also unopposed for his post. The 1961 editor hails from Boise, Idaho, and is currently associate editor in charge of organizations section of the Bijou. He is planning to major in economics.

In other Transcript selections, freshman Mike Maharry was named managing editor, over other candidates Jack Donnan, Tom Grissom and Terry Swango.

Dick Lacy, a sophomore from Cleveland, O., was elected business manager of the newspaper over Bob Barr, junior.

Maharry is currently student government editor, and comes from Dearborn, Mich.

Lacy served as assistant treasurer of his fraternity and on the Bijou business staff.

articles.headline: Professors To Consider Compromise Test Plan
articles.body:
A compromise on bluebook-scheduling policy, worked out between student and faculty committees, will go to the Faculty meeting Monday night. The compromise would allow faculty members to change bluebook dates that fall within two or three days before or after Monnett and fall Homecoming week ends, according to former Student Body President Bryce Collier.

The student Academic Relations Committee had previously proposed that bluebooks be banned on those days, but the faculty General Academic Committee rejected that proposal.

Under the compromise plan, teachers with classes meeting at 8 MWF, 10 MWF, 1:10 MWF, 3:10 MWF, 8 TThS, 9 TThS, 10 TThS, 11 TThS, 1:10 TTh and 2:10 TTh could reschedule their examinations so as not to fall immediately before or after the holiday week ends, Collier added.

articles.headline: Court Seeks Rule Change
articles.author: Mike Maharry Student Government Editor
articles.body:
An addition to the student Government by-laws prohibiting Men's Court justices from running for IFC Executive Council, Student Council or Elections and Safety Committee chairmanships was recommended by Men's Court, Chief Justice Roger Thaler said last week.

The recommendation was to have been acted upon by Student Council last night, according to SC President George Conrades.

"Under the court's recommendation, any member of Men's Court who is a candidate for these positions," Thaler explained, "must resign from the court and can not be reappointed." If approved by Council, the recommendation will be sent for approval to an "organ of the faculty," probably Dean Ingraham, and will go into effect immediately.

Division Of Power

Thaler said that the recommendation was being made to insure the division of power between the executive and judicial branches of Student Government.

He also said that the recommendation would make sure that Men's Court would not be used as a "stepping stone" for political aspirants.

Justice Jon Denney, newly-elected IFC president, will resign from the court later this year, but Bob Maxwell and Bob Richardson, both defeated in their races for student body president and representative-at-large, respectively, will not be affected by the ruling, Thaler said.

Plan Not New

According to Thaler, the court's recommendation is not a new one, but was in the SG constitution up until two years ago. At that time, the constitution was revised and the Men's Court eligibility ruling was left out. Since then the court has made several recommendations, but none have been incorporated into the constitution or the by-laws.

The chairmen of the Elections and Safety Committees have been included in the recommendation, Thaler explained, because they, along with members of the IFC Executive Council and Student Council, have the power to bring charges to Men's Court.

"It would not uphold democratic principles to have people bringing charges to court and also trying the cases as members of the court," Thaler said.

Conrades told the Transcript last week that he is in favor of the court's recommendation and that he felt the proposal would strengthen the court's position on campus.

articles.headline: Deferred Pledging Plan OK'd By Greek Prexies
articles.body:
Part of the deferred pledging proposal requiring freshmen to attend all 12 fraternity houses during Rush Week was approved by the Fraternity Presidents' Assembly when both old and new Interfraternity Council officers met last Wednesday.

According to Al Alexander, outgoing IFC secretary, the first part of the proposal was generally accepted, but opinion was split on the second part requiring freshmen to go to the fraternity houses, instead of the Greeks seeking out the freshmen as in the present system.

The proposal will be returned to the Executive Council for consideration and any alternate proposals will be presented at FPA's next meeting.

In other FPA action John Keltner, Circle K president, presented the IFC Treasurers' Committee proposal to abolish fraternities' financing Circle K meals for their members.

A motion to halt the Treasurers' Committee investigation and continue the present system was passed, Alexander said.

articles.headline: Honorary Degree Conferred On DAL
articles.body:
President David A. Lockmiller will receive the honorary degree of Doctor of Literature from the University of Chattanooga Friday at the inauguration of his successor at the school, LeRoy A. Martin.

President Lockmiller had been the ninth president at Chattanooga before coming to OWU as its tenth president. His citation will be given in recognition of his work as a scholar and productive author as well as a nationally known educator, the university announced.

Besides serving as Ohio Wesleyan's president, President Lockmiller was recently elected president of the Association of American Colleges, which includes 95 per cent of the accredited, four-year liberal arts institutions in the nation.

President Lockmiller has written five books: "Magoon in Cuba: 1906-1909," "Sir William Blackstone," "History of the North Carolina State College of Agricultural and Engineering," "The Consolidation of the University of North Carolina" and "Enoch H. Crowder: Soldier, Lawyer and Statesman," in addition to numerous book reviews in historical and educational journals.

He also served as editor of "Proceedings of the Southern University Conference" from 1956-59. President Lockmiller is by profession a lawyer and a teacher. This is his 18th year as a college president.

The degree from Chattanooga will be his third honorary award. He has received the degree of Doctor of Laws from Emory University and from Cumberland University.

articles.headline: Male Counselor Applications Out
articles.body:
Applications for positions as student counselors in Men's Residence Halls No. 1, No. 2 and in the East Selby dormitory are available beginning today in the Dean of Men's office, an announcement from that office disclosed last week.

Applications will be available through next Wednesday and must be returned to the office of the dean by Mar. 31. Appointments will be made and applicants notified by Apr. 16.

Sixteen counselors are needed to staff the three halls — six in Hall No. 1, seven in Hall No. 2 and three in East Selby. The positions are open to upperclassmen who will be juniors or seniors next year, the announcement said.

articles.headline: Busy Week For Greeks Scheduled: Scholarship Theme Planned For Banquet
articles.body:
A scholarship theme will be carried out for the Greek Week Banquet to be held tomorrow at 6 p.m. in the MUB Ballroom.

John Sagan, a 1948 graduate of OWU and assistant treasurer of the Ford Motor Company, will be the speaker for the banquet. While he attended OWU, Sagan was a member of Phi Beta Kappa, Phi Kappa Phi, Delta Sigma Rho, Omicron Delta Kappa and Phi Gamma Delta. He received his master's degree in economics and later his Ph.D. from the University of Illinois. At present Sagan is a member of the OWU Alumni Board of Directors.

Dave Ross, outgoing IFC president, will serve as toastmaster for the banquet, at which time the fraternity and sorority scholarship trophies will be presented.

The Greek Week carnival will be held Friday from 8-10 p.m. in Edwards Gym. Each fraternity will be paired with a sorority in presenting some game or activity during the carnival.

Saturday night Edwards Gym will be the scene of the Greek Week Ball, from 8:30 p.m.-12:30 a.m. The Brothers Four will be featured at the dance and music for dancing will be provided by Lou Posey and his band.

The Sorority Song Fest will be held Sunday in Gray Chapel at 8:15 p.m. The contest songs are "Black is the Color of My True Love's Hair," "Red Rosey Bush," "Good Night" and "Prayer from Hansel and Gretel." Judges will be Taylor from Capitol University, Ferris Ohl from Heidelberg University and David Miller from Wittenberg University.

Two trophies will be presented to the winning sorority this year. Mu Phi Epsilon, women's music honorary, will present a rotating trophy, donated by the Campus Music Store, C. J. articles.headline: MUB Opens Otten Show
articles.body:
The Albert Otten Collection of 14 paintings opened yesterday for a month's exhibition at the MUB. This exhibition has been shown only two times before in public, at Brandeis University and Drew University.

Robert Vickers, assistant professor of fine arts, said that the exhibition was obtained directly from Otten's home and will not be shown elsewhere in the surrounding area.

Artists whose paintings are included in the collection are Courbet, Derain, Dufy, Ensor, Gauguin, Kokoschka, Munch, Nolde, Pascin, Pechstein, Renoir, Signac and Vlaminck. These paintings were shipped secretly out of Germany when Otten was forced to flee because of Nazi persecution.

articles.headline: Soviet SC Invites OWU
articles.body:
The "Student Council of the USSR" has sent Ohio Wesleyan an invitation to attend a summer school for student government participants in the Crimea in July.

Student Body President Bryce Collier announced at last Tuesday's Student Council meeting that he had received a letter from the Soviet organization asking him to send delegates.

According to the letter, delegates will stay at the International Youth and Student Camp at Gurzuf July 1-12 and will move to Moscow for a similar program July 14-17.

The program will include meetings and talks with Soviet scientists and cultural workers, trips within the Crimea, yachting and a trip to the "hero city" of Sevastopol.

Collier commented briefly on the letter at the Mar. 8 Student Council meeting. He felt it would be "unlikely" that Ohio Wesleyan would send any delegates.

articles.headline: Forgotten Faculty Plan Bears Re-Examination
articles.body:
Two years ago, a faculty committee concerned with encouraging students to the “superior efforts which lie within their abilities” suggested a reorganization of the academic structure of the University. Although realizing that such a change could not provide a total answer to the problem, the committee presented a curriculum alteration to reduce many of the obstacles to superior academic work,

THE COMMITTEE made the following observations: 1) Because each student carries “an excessive number” of separate courses, “his studies become overly fragmented, discouraging study in sufficient depth in any single course.”

2) Fragmentation of faculty efforts results from “excessive time spent in conferring with large numbers of students, grading examinations and preparing for separate classes which prevents the use of that time in longer individual conferences, qualitative improvement of course content and scholarly advancement.”

3) At present, students are “frequently allowed to continue into upper-level courses when their work in the freshman and sophomore years lends serious doubt as to their ability to do advanced work.”

4) Independent study and research is “not, perhaps as much a part of the normal program as might be desirable.” (Of 36 senior candidates for B.A. degrees in 1958 having point averages over 3.3, only nine were enrolled in a 496 course for the spring semester.)

5) In addition to allowing students to receive a degree without a sufficient check of their “total attainment” of the University’s objectives, the present plan “probably results in students’ considering each course an entity . . unrelated to the total educational program.”

THESE THINGS ARE JUST as true in 1960 as they were in 1958, but aside from this year’s lifting of the comprehensive exam plan out of the context of the committee’s total recommendation, the project petered out after the faculty vote.

Attempting to rejuvenate last autumn’s leaves, we would like to review the suggestions of the 1958 faculty.

To meet the first two deficiencies listed above, the committee suggested that the “four-course system” or a variant of it merited “careful consideration.” Requiring a more intensive planning of course content, the plan would reduce the student’s semester load to four courses; and 32 courses, rather than 124 semester hours, would be required for graduation.

Although this was only a tentative and preliminary study on the part of the faculty, and we realize the enormous problems any such extensive curriculum revision creates, we would enthusiastically encourage a further investigation in the same general direction with a view to making Ohio Wesleyan’s academic program an even more valuable tool in the production of graduates capable of original and creative thinking and possessing a superior education.

Given the potential in the present student body, faculty and Administration, plus the intellectual challenge extended to a small, high quality, liberal arts college today, there is every reason why OWU should start planning in this direction.

articles.headline: Long-Range Class Gift Deserves Full Support
articles.body:
Last year’s senior class adopted an endowment plan as a long-range capital gift to the University. This plan, by insuring the lives of a number of class members, will, in 1984, mature as a $40,000 sum to be presented to Ohio Wesleyan. This year the Class of 1960 has again adopted this means of helping to insure that the University will have future means for expansion and improvement of facilities.

IN THE NEXT FEW WEEKS the plan will be presented to the seniors by the Class Gift Committee. This marks the second time that such a gift has been set up by an OWU class prior to its graduation.

Other colleges dependent on alumni contributions for income have for many years maintained a plan of this sort. We should hope that the step undertaken by last year’s seniors will be carried on and expanded by this year’s class. The goal is $100,000 worth of policies, to mature at the Class of 1960’s 25th reunion, in 1985. The individual expense is small, and it is only through this type of plan that a really substantial sum can be made available to the University for capital improvements by a number of its alumni.

WE URGE ACTIVE support of the plan by this year’s senior class and continuance of the policy by future classes. Only through willing support of its program by its alumni can Ohio Wesleyan continue to offer the high quality of service it has traditionally made available to its students.

articles.headline: Lack Of Censorship Is Paper's Blessing
articles.author: Jerry Sell
articles.body:
Open Opinions

Transcript Columnist

The word “censor” has a Latin root related to the word “to think.” So literally, when one is censored he is kept from thinking, or he lets someone else, the censor, do his thinking for him.

We all know that censorship is often a bad thing. One of the worst types of censorship is censorship of a college or university newspaper by the school administration.

Never is “censoring” (that is, restriction of thinking) more out of place than in a university, a place dedicated (to use a cliche) to “thinking for yourself.”

Thanks Called For
At Ohio Wesleyan we ought to interrupt our customary griping long enough to appreciate the complete freedom given the Transcript by the Administration.

This freedom has important implications, for there are times when such freedom could be a source of embarrassment to the Administration.

To cite an hypothetical case, suppose an able young instructor, a truly excellent teacher, were to be dismissed because of some power struggle among the Administration, or even because of budgetary considerations.

Voice Thinking
The Transcript would be able to voice the “thinking” of the students, to state their case, to say it is most unfortunate for the University to let such factors determine tenure of instructors.

The paper could stir up quite a bit of trouble pointing out that this man’s dismissal would not only hurt the University, but would hurt all the students who would otherwise have profited from his teaching, not to mention the inconvenience to the young man himself.

Many Censored
Many schools would not tolerate such open criticism in the college newspaper. But, again, here we can be grateful for an Administration which realizes that the student, too, should have a voice in the conduct of the University’s affairs.

After all, the students are the reason for the institution’s existence.

Editor, the Transcript:

After reading “Showdown On Civil Rights Battle” (the Open Opinion of March 9), I must advance a criticism on the idealistic and almost fire and brimstone approaches of the columnist (and most Americans, unfortunately).

When and where there is a friction among men, dissention over the grievance cannot and will not be settled to the benefit of the parties involved unless it is agreed by and acted upon mutually.

The only workable solution to the Negro and white, North and South, and many other problems of our idealistic Nation, will rest upon the unshakeable foundations of Time, Education, and Understanding — not upon “Showdowns.”

articles.headline: ---And a twist of lemon peel.
articles.author: Max Shulman
articles.body:
First of all, we will take up the matter of diet. In the past, babies were raised largely on table scraps. This, however, was outlawed by the Smoot-Hawley Act, and today babies are fed a scientific formula consisting of dextrose, maltose, distilled water, evaporated milk and a twist of lemon peel.

After eating, the baby tends to grow sleepy. A lullaby is very useful to help it fall asleep. In case you don't know any lullabies, make one up. This is not at all difficult. In a lullaby the words are unimportant since the baby doesn't understand them anyhow. The important thing is the sound. All you have to do is string together a bunch of nonsense syllables, taking care that they make an agreeable sound. For example:
Go to sleep, my little infant,
Goo-goo moo-moo poo-poo binfant.

Having fed and serenaded the baby, arrange it in the position for slumber. A baby sleeps best on its stomach so place it that way in its crib. Then to make sure it will not turn itself over during the night lay a soft but fairly heavy object on its back—another baby, for instance.

articles.headline: YW Names Junior For Russian Trip
articles.body:
Ursula Parrish, junior psychology major, has been chosen as one of approximately twenty YWCA-chosen students to go to Russia this summer. Her application was accepted less than two weeks after she sent it to the National YWCA-Board in New York.

Miss Parrish will leave New York City on July 3 and fly to Paris, France, where the group will spend three days, then go on to Prague, Czechoslovakia. They will leave Prague July 9 by train and arrive in Chop, just over the Russian border.

There the group will split into thirds. Accompanied by a Russian guide most of the time, they plan to visit a few major Russian cities such as Moscow and Stalingrad. Greatest hope for direct communication with Soviet young people is the one "sports camp" on the agenda.

Leaving Russia Aug. 19 by the city of Reni, her group will enter Rumania and spend a few days at Bucharest, Rumania. From there they will go to Vienna, Austria, and on into East Germany, where they will spend three days in an evaluation session near Nuremberg.

Miss Parrish will then stay about three days in Paris, France, before flying back to New York.

The $1,300 project will be mostly a matter of personal expense, Miss Parrish said, although she is exploring the possibility of aid from interested groups.

Out of an extensive study program the YWCA has prepared for their Russia-bound group, each person is supposed to specialize in one area. This study includes language, literature and art of both countries, their histories, their philosophies, their theories and machineries of government, economics, structures of society, party attitudes and especially knowledge of current events.

The week before the plane leaves New York, she will be subjected to an orientation week, hearing scholars and persons connected with East-West exchange, studying how best to make contact with the Russian people.

In a recent YW meeting here on campus Miss Parrish met with Executive Director Miriam Wiley, last year's community ambassador Roger Thaler, new ambassador Rosh Doan, outgoing YW president Judith Blackburn, District Deputy Elaine Flory, Margie MacLeod, chairman of the International Understanding Committee of the YW, and new YW President Karen Doud.

They decided to form a weekly group to discuss Russia and either Nigeria or India, according to which one is finally chosen for the new community ambassador.

Miss Parrish, 20, is the daughter of the sociology head of the University of Louisville. She plans to attend graduate school in the fields of child guidance and psychology. At the present time she is the vice-president and social chairman of the 112 Co-op House, a member of Orchesis and was an Independent representative in Pan-Hellenic the fall of her sophomore year.

articles.headline: Sledding Diverts Coeds On Stuyvesant's Slopes
articles.author: Pat Hanna Transcript Staff
articles.body:
There are many ways of avoiding homework, but one of the most intriguing lately has been sledding on the hill in front of Stuyvesant Hall. Due to the recent cold weather, the hill has been coated with a shining layer of hard-packed snow.

The word sledding may be inappropriate, since sleds are rather scarce among OWU students. In their place, trays, dish pans and even pieces of cardboard are substituted.

Mishaps have run low. Among those reported, other than bruises and "sore muscles," were various torn coats and a pair of badly mangled glasses.

However, the spirit remains, especially to a jolly few who, at 6 a.m. one day, were seen and definitely heard having a great time on the slope beneath the windows of sleeping freshmen.

If you're in a daring mood, you might try, as some do, to stand up on the tray as it glides recklessly downward to steer between two well-placed trees or form a group of 10 or more people and see who's still with you when you reach the bottom.

A fitting climax is the bump which appears just as you have reached full speed. When you finally arrive back on firm ground, you may have decided to sit — or maybe stand — the next one out.

articles.headline: Debaters Get 2nd In NOC
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan's debate team placed second out of a 15-team field in the Northeast Ohio Conference Debate Tournament held last Saturday at Akron, O., team member Blake Schubert told the Transcript early this week.

Losing only to the winner of the tournament, Western Reserve University, of Cleveland O., the OWU squad compiled a 5-1 record in debating the national collegiate topic, "Should Congress have the power to reverse decisions of the Supreme Court?"

The negative team of Charles Mills and Judy Strayer won all three of their rounds, stretching their winning string for the season to seven straight. Earlier in the season, in a tournament at DePaul University, Greencastle, Ind., Mills was named outstanding speaker in the competition, Schubert added.

Vincent Murphy and Schubert, debating the affirmative for OWU, defeated Case Tech and Bowling Green, losing only to Western Reserve, the eventual winner of the tournament.

Commented OWU debate coach Edward R. Robinson, associate professor of speech, "I was pleasantly surprised at Akron. We certainly were not one of the pre-tournament favorites."

Of the total of 45 rounds at Akron, 32 were won by teams debating the negative, 13 by the affirmative, Schubert concluded.

articles.headline: Ionesco Experiments 'Unusual' For OWU
articles.author: Linda Merkle Transcript Staff
articles.body:
Eugene Ionesco's plays, "The Lesson" and "The Bald Soprano," were presented by the Wesleyan Players last Wednesday through Saturday. These presentations were the most unusual to appear at Ohio Wesleyan yet this year.

Ionesco is an experimental playwright. He attempts to convey in his work the inanity of life. By pushing farce, burlesque and parody to their furthest, he attempts to reach the heights of real tragedy. Here, he believes, is true theater.

There are diverse opinions on the worth of Ionesco's plays. Brooks Atkinson calls him "provocative." Richard Watts calls his work "hollow and pretentious fakery."

"The Lesson" is a play symbolizing education carried to the ridiculous. It presents a humble professor attempting to instruct a student in the basic philosophies of life. The play ends with the professor destroying the pupil out of impatience with her stupidity and errotic desire for her youth.

Ronald Anderson's portrayal of the professor in "The Lesson" was the triumph of the evening. His delivery was excellent. His actions were violent and portrayed madness with realism.

Suzanne Whitney was a little too cloying as the pupil. Even though the role called for this sweetness, she overacted considerably.

Linda Kramer, although a trifle strained, was good in her supporting role.

In "The Bald Soprano" Ionesco tells of the stupidity and lack of communication between man and wife and between man and his surroundings. He does this by parodying the conversations and lives of middle-class Englishmen.

Jo Ann Gerwick was excellent as the typically inane English wife in "The Bald Soprano." Her diction and posture throughout the play were superb.

James Guimond, the visiting husband, along with Susan Smith, his wife, were adequate in their roles. Guimond seemed rather weak in the early stages of the play. However, he improved as the play progressed. Miss Smith shone in the snoring scene in the final portion of the play.

Ron Parady, as Miss Gerwick's husband, was difficult to understand at the beginning, but gave an excellent performance overall.

Trish Dressel and Matthew Finkin were satisfactory in their roles.

Congratulations are deserved by Sarah Blackmun for the excellent make-up work.

It is a shame that the audience appreciated only the broader humor. They missed many of the more subtle speeches of the evening, although the plays were very well received as a whole. One wonders if the plays were understood in the tragic overtones or enjoyed only for their humor.

Donald Eyssen, associate professor of speech, announced that the plays will be presented for the Theta Alpha Phi, national drama honorary, convention at Purdue during spring vacation and in Cleveland, for the Monnett Club there later this year.

articles.headline: Conference End Sought
articles.body:
A recommendation to disband the Five College Conference Committee was made last Tuesday at the last meeting of this year's Student Council.

The recommendation, unanimously approved by the council, will now be sent to the incoming council with the additional suggestion that a new "College Conference Committee" be formed in place of the old committee.

The council felt that the social and political structure of several of the Five College Conference schools was too far removed from that of OWU's to be of sufficient value to the school.

Jane Polley, this year's Five College Conference Committee chairman, told the Transcript last week that she was in complete agreement with the recommendation. She said that it was made at her suggestion, and that she hoped to see a new type of inter-school committee formed in its place.

Student Body President George Conrades, who presided over his newly-elected Student Council for the first time last night, said, "I, too, would be in favor of drawing from schools more similar to ours, like Denison."

articles.headline: OWU Offers Swap Plan
articles.body:
Women students interested in participating in Ohio Wesleyan's semester exchange with one of three Negro colleges in the South next fall should contact Russell E. Bayliff, professor of sociology, before Mar. 23.

Bennett College for Women, Greensboro, N.C.; Hampton Institute, a coed college in Hampton, Va., and Spelman College, the women's division of Atlanta (Ga.) University are the participating schools, Prof. Bayliff said.

Three OWU coeds participated in the exchange program last year. Marilyn Todd, senior from Silver Spring, Md., and Charlene Beale, senior from Dayton, O., both attended Hampton Institute. Mary Ellen Bender, Leonia, N.J., attended Bennett College, where she is presently finishing her undergraduate training.

One woman student from each of the participating Negro colleges was here last year.

Tuition and fees are paid to OWU, with room and board being paid to the college attended. Students on scholarships retain their standing, Prof. Bayliff added.

Before leaving, the student would work out a suitable schedule with her adviser to assure proper credit transfer and maintenance of work in the major field, Prof. Bayliff concluded.

articles.headline: Journalist To Lecture
articles.body:
John R. Beal, Time Magazine's diplomatic correspondent in Washington, will deliver this year's Outstanding Journalist lectures at OWU.

Beal will deliver the Student Publications Banquet address at the Fort Delaware Hotel Tuesday night, Apr. 19, and then address Chapel Wednesday morning.

The 1926 graduate of Ohio Wesleyan has spent 32 years in news work, including a quarter of a century with the Washington bureaus of United Press, Newsweek and Time. In 1946, Beal undertook a 14-month mission as adviser to Chinese Nationalist President Chiang Kai-shek and his cabinet in Nanking. The mission was arranged by the late Gen. George C. Marshall.

Wrote Dulles Biography

Beal's 1957 biography of John Foster Dulles, which was reviewed in all major U.S. publications, was re-published in a revised edition by Harper & Brothers last November.

His work as diplomatic correspondent has taken him abroad once or twice a year since 1950. During his service in China, he became personally acquainted with Red China's Premier Chou En-lai, who was then head of the Communist delegation in Nanking.

After graduation from OWU, Beal spent two years in newspaper work in Elyria, O., and Paterson, N.J., before beginning a five-year stint with United Press in New York. He was moved to UP's Washington bureau in 1934 and during the next eight years filled such posts as chief of UP's House and Senate staffs.

Covered Whitehouse

He joined the staff of Newsweek in 1942 and two years later shifted to Time. Prior to becoming diplomatic correspondent in 1950, he worked on other major Washington beats, including coverage of the White House during President Truman's tenure.

Beal's mother, Bessie Robinson Beal, '03, spent more than 30 years with Ohio Wesleyan's Alumni Office. At the 1958 Commencement, she was one of four alumni honored for outstanding service to OWU.

articles.headline: Committee Discusses OWU Honor System
articles.body:
Pros and cons of an honor system for Ohio Wesleyan were aired Friday by a temporary Student Council committee.

"Our main task is to investigate student opinion to see what kind of an honor system is needed here", chairman Jerry Sell told the Transcript. According to Sell, the effectiveness of any type of honor system at OWU would depend upon the support and attitude of the student body.

Dean of the University George W. Burns said that plans of an honor system have been discussed "in various quarters once every college generation." No proposal has come to a formal vote.

The committee plans to discuss the merits of various systems from area colleges. Denison University and Oberlin, Antioch and Wooster colleges are now using honor plans.

Discussion implied that an ideal honor system entails two responsibilities: reporting one's own violations and reporting the violations of fellow students.

Before adopting such a plan, Ohio Wesleyan students would have to consider 1) Would a student report himself? 2) Would he report a friend? 3) "We want to see what actually happens there," Sell said.

The 51-year-old honor system at Oberlin College applies to "all work handed in for academic credit." Denison University students are to vote on extending their system to academic work as well as living rules, Robert H. Ross, associate professor of English and adviser to the committee, said.

Antioch College's plan reportedly covers both academic and living rules.

How serious a moral offense would be a breach of honor?

Non-proctored exams and AWS regulations present a partial honor system at OWU, the committee pointed out. However, "students sometimes fall through, because in other areas they aren't on their honor," committee member Barbara Follmer added.

"No honor system will work perfectly," Prof. Ross concluded. "It's got to come from the students, if at all."

articles.headline: Expressway Plans Roll
articles.body:
Delaware City Council is currently taking steps toward the construction of an expressway to relieve the "heavy and dangerous" traffic through Delaware, Don Mackley, city manager, reported to the Transcript last week.

According to Mackley, the south interchange of the proposed expressway will be located below Rip's Drive-In at a point where present Route 42 will be relocated to meet Route 23. The expressway will swing north to a point two blocks east of Sandusky Street, then veer northwest along the west bank of the Olentangy River to rejoin present Route 23 north of the city. Route 42 will swing off Mingo Park and intersect present Route 23 by Greenwood Lake.

When asked if the new expressway would interfere with University property, Mackley stated that it may hit the southwest corner of South Field, taking a minute portion off the soccer field.

A bond issue, which must be passed before actual construction begins, will probably be presented to Delaware voters in November, according to Prof. Sell Bayliff, professor of sociology and Delaware city clerk. The last bond issue for the expressway, which was presented in November, 1958, fell eight per cent short of the necessary majority vote.

Prof. Bayliff reported that the entire project would cost Delaware an estimated 6.5 million dollars, but with the cooperation of the state of Ohio the cost could be reduced to ten thousands dollars.

articles.headline: Housemother Named For 'Mother Of Year'
articles.author: Ronnie Ruch Community Affairs Ed.
articles.body:
Mrs. Dewey Talley, Phi Gamma Delta housemother, was recently nominated as a candidate for Ohio's "Mother of the Year" by the Progressive Mother's Club of Delaware.

If Mrs. Talley is selected from other nominees in Ohio, she will be considered for the title of "American Mother of the Year." Contestants for the national competition will represent the 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico.

Mrs. Talley, who has resided in Delaware since 1936, is the mother of four children and the grandmother of eight. Her son, John Robert, a senior football star at Northwestern University, was named "Midwest Back of the Week" after his performance against Notre Dame last fall.

Mrs. Talley served as president of the Women's Association of the First Presbyterian Church from 1952-56. She has also directed a private kindergarten in her home for the past 10 years.

The three letters of reference required by the state selection committee were written in Mrs. Talley's behalf by the Rev. Mr. Louis Campbell, minister at First Presbyterian Church, Carl Hopkins, superintendent of Delaware schools, and Robert Meyer, former city councilman and OWU controller.

OWU has never been represented at the conference, which has been held for the past six years on the Indiana campus.

articles.headline: Press Box
articles.author: Rog Lockwood
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan, like every other college, has its own unique peculiarities. Where else would you find a president’s house that looks like a Howard Johnson’s; a contrived, expansive and remarkably ineffectual complex of faculty committees and rush week programs, and an unbecoming catalogue clause that pertains to a non-existant code of unstated standards?

And where else would you see a more unique spring training arrangement, with the baseball team fielding and throwing on the gym basketball floor, the hitters slamming tennis balls off the walls on the handball courts and the lacrosse team consigned to South Field Siberia?

The only team in its proper element is the track squad, which utilizes the darkened track above Les Michael’s war zone, where pseudo baseballs fill the air like the cross-fire on a military beachhead. And the tennis players, deprived of a home, have been discussing their season in the MUB.

Top honors for originality and aptness of thought must go to Lacrosse Coach Fred Myers, however, who plowed out a playing area for his courageous band of 35 or more and leads them to his glacial arena every day of the week, in fair weather or foul.

To overcome climatic handicaps such as thickly falling snow and zero visibility, Fred is attired in a bright red hat (which serves as a warning beacon) and a loud whistle that lets his snowmen know when practice has started — and when it’s over.

So far, frostbite and snowblindness have been the only real hazards, and nearly everyone gets back to the Selby Stadium locker room when practice is over.

Myers anticipates a good season if and when the snow melts. One thing is certain: bad weather isn’t going to cancel any chances to practice.

Yes, the spring training sites are unique here in the Squaw Valley of the Mid-West, but maybe it won’t always be this way. After all, with the Williams Drive area seething with construction activity it may come to pass that a field house might be erected, too.

All it takes is money and time, and we’ve got plenty of time.

articles.headline: Bishop Trackmen Cop Third Place In OC Meet
articles.body:
A strong effort by the Ohio Wesleyan track team fell just short of winning the Ohio Conference Indoor Track Championship. The Bishops tallied 31 1/4 to finish third.

The Bishops were in contention for the title until the final event, the mile relay. In the mile relay, Capital scored four points to give them 35 1/2 and first in the meet. Wooster picked up five points for 34 1/2 and second. The Bishops failed to score.

A brilliant individual effort by Art Slate of Capital enabled the Lutherans to take the crown. Slate won three events and ran a key leg on the mile relay.

Three OWU Firsts

OWU picked up three first places in the meet. Gold medals were won by John Guy, Dave Ross and Don Bourquard.

Topping all Bishop performances was a feat of stamina and skill seldom performed by a freshman, Paul Wennermark, who placed second in both the mile and two-mile runs. Wennermark showed determination and promise in tallying eight points for the OWU cause.

John Guy defeated a fast field in the 55-yard dash. The first three finishers were separated by less than a yard.

Ross Wins 440

After three years of running in the shadow of Bob Davis, Dave Ross finally took a much-deserved first place in the 440-yard dash. Ross led all the way for his win.

Don Bourquard proved that only Gutknecht had kept him from a gold medal, as he took the two-mile run for the Bishops. Bourquard turned on a strong finishing kick to win the event.

Doug Cotterman and Dick Gillespie were other scorers for the Ohio Wesleyan team. Cotterman took second in the shot put and tied for fourth in the pole vault. Gillespie sailed 6 ft. to take second in the high jump.

The favored Wooster team suffered heavily from the loss of Craig Taylor due to an injury. With Taylor, it appears, they easily would have won the meet.

Slate's triple win came in the high and low hurdles and the broad jump. Pete Lund of Oberlin won the high jump, Bob Gill of Akron, the 880. Gary Allen of Otterbein captured first in the shot put. Wooster won both the mile and 880 relays.

articles.headline: Livingston Relays Held On Saturday
articles.body:
Track fans among OWU students will get a chance to see some top-flight competition this week end. OWU's track team will participate in the annual Livingston Relays.

Saturday evening the Livingston Relays will be held in the Denison Field House, Granville, O. The field will include the top track men in the Mid-West.

Heading the field will be Hayes Jones of Eastern Michigan. Jones, the toast of the indoor season, has captured impressive wins in the hurdles against the best in the USA.

Western Michigan will field a strong team. They have a replacement for the incomparable Ira Murchison in Joel Johnson. Johnson, an upset winner in the recent Michigan Relays, is expected to duel Jones for the sprint crown.

articles.headline: Lettermen Bolster Golf Team Hopes
articles.body:
Experience, intrasquad competition and a little bit of luck are the factors that could bring Ohio Wesleyan's golf team a conference championship and a fine season, as coach Dick Gordin's linksmen prepare for the spring campaign.

With only Tates Locke missing from last year's squad that finished in a tie for third in the conference, Coach Gordin believes that he has the experience and depth for a championship contender.

The returning lettermen are Rod Myers, Jud Sayre, Jim Tennison, Rick Schaal, Jack Winters and Gene Cawood. Also back after a year's absence is Chris terKuile, who qualified number one during the fall tryouts.

Coach Gordin indicated that the team has fine balance this year, and that competition will be very intense for the top four positions on the team. Based on fall qualifying scores, terKuile finished first with a 48-hole score of 224. He was followed by Myers with 226, Sayre with 238 and Tennison with 239.

Close on the heels of the top four were Schaal—240, freshman Gary Schaal—242, Winters—242 and Cawood—243. Other freshmen who looked good were Chuck Wilson and John Moody.

Coach Gordin thinks that the conference crown will probably be won by OWU, Denison or Wittenberg. Denison, last year's champion, has a veteran team and Wittenberg will have the advantage of its home course when the conference championships are played.

With some luck here and there, it could be a very profitable season for Coach Gordin and his veteran squad of linksmen, who open their schedule against Denison on Apr. 15.

articles.headline: Lacrosse Team Will Field Strongest Squad
articles.body:
The Ohio Wesleyan lacrosse team is looking forward to what should be the best season in Ohio Wesleyan history.

With 49 men on the roster, of which 13 are returning letter winners, Coach Fred Myers is confident that he has exceptional strength at every position. According to Myers, "The biggest problem is to get all the experience and ability on the field at the same time."

After a sub-freezing scrimmage last Saturday, Coach Myers commented, "We're big, we're rough and we're fast. We have tremendous potential, and I know we'll go a long way."

Starting in the goal will be Thorpe Mitchell, a fourth year man who was all-conference his sophomore year. Close behind him is sophomore Terry Dougherty.

The defense is led by co-captain Phil Roos and averages well over 6 ft. and close to 220 lbs. per man.

At midfield, Myers is swamped with 12 players who have all experienced at least one year of competition.

Senior Rog Auker will lead the attack as set-up man for freshman Jeff Fox and junior Bill Bishop. Fighting at their heels for a position are Tom Howell, Dick Weist and Dave Berger.

While seeking to better last year's three won-eight lost record, the Bishops will face Oberlin, last year's conference champions, and Rensselaer, a perennial powerhouse from upstate New York.

articles.headline: SOME PLAIN TALK FROM A DOCTOR ABOUT PROJECT HOPE
articles.body:
Over the years, many members of my profession have shared their skills generously with people in other lands. In the main, however, their efforts have been extended individually—or in small groups.

Now Project HOPE is asking all Americans to join in a large scale health effort involving the work of hundreds of doctors. These doctors will contribute their skills in a project as imaginative, as bold, and as far-reaching as any that comes to mind. Its base will be a fully-equipped, fully-staffed hospital ship—the S.S. HOPE—which will serve as a floating health center. With the support of the American people behind it, the ship will sail for Southeast Asia in 1960.

Naturally, we doctors are enthusiastic about HOPE. It is a practical application of the highest ideals of our oath. My colleagues at the A.M.A. have endorsed it, as has almost everybody from President Eisenhower on down. Some 2,000 medical specialists have volunteered to serve.

Beyond this, however, at least three facts about HOPE especially concern you. First, wherever the S.S. HOPE calls, it will help others to help themselves. That means that our efforts will be directed primarily toward training doctors, nurses, and other medical and health people. And that means your contribution will be multiplied many times over, for those who will be trained by us will, in turn, be able to pass this training on in the months and years ahead.

Second, HOPE's effect will not be limited to its medical objectives. Its scope and approach assure that. We will have here an effective means for making and keeping international friends.

Finally, HOPE is not an "official" project. As a people-to-people undertaking, it will clearly express the deep concern of the American people for the peoples of other lands. As such, it couldn't be more worthy of your contribution. A dollar will help so much. And it can come back to you in so many worthwhile ways.
